tn.w3:s: ไวน์สปาร์กลิง
tn.w3:o: ไวน์เสริมแอลกอฮอล์

qs.q: Why is a Rioja Reserva usually 'developing' when released?
o: It has already been aged before release
It is made with a share of dried grapes
It is fermented oxidatively in part-filled casks
It is bottled without filtration or sulfites
qs.e: Development measures the balance of primary/secondary against tertiary aromas, so a wine may no longer be 'youthful' when released. Red Rioja Reservas, for example, are aged before release and usually show some tertiary aromas, so on sale they are 'developing'. They are not from dried grapes, not always oxidised and are oak-aged.

qs.q: What does over-chilling do to whites, rosés and sparkling wines?
o: It masks the flavours
It increases fruitiness
It increases sweetness
It has no effect
qs.e: Ice buckets and coolers keep whites, rosés and sparkling wines cold, but over-chilling can mask their flavours: aromas and taste are perceived less when wine is too cold. It does not increase fruitiness or sweetness, and there is an effect.

qs.q: Why is a grape variety not propagated from seed?
o: A seedling is a new variety, different from its parents
Grape seeds never germinate because their coat is too thick
Because EU law forbids it for every vinifera vine
Because the plant would grow too fast and bear no fruit
qs.e: To preserve a variety's unique qualities, seeds cannot be used: a seed results from fertilisation and gives a plant with different genetics from its parents, i.e. a new variety (even if both parents are the same variety). So vines are propagated by cuttings or layering, giving identical plants. Grape seeds do germinate, it is not illegal and not too fast (it is slow).

qs.q: Why can maritime Bordeaux ripen Cabernet Sauvignon?
o: Temperatures stay warm enough for ripening to continue far into autumn
Summers are very hot and dry, with temperatures often above 35 °C
It almost never rains between flowering and harvest, thanks to the Atlantic
Black volcanic soils store heat and release it to the grapes at night
qs.e: Maritime climates have cool to moderate temperatures and little difference between hottest and coldest months (low continentality), with rain spread through the year moderating temperature. So it stays warm enough for ripening to continue far into autumn: hence maritime Bordeaux can ripen thick-skinned Cabernet Sauvignon, which might otherwise struggle at that latitude. It is not very hot summers, no rain or volcanic soils.

qs.q: Which statement about irrigation is true?
o: Drip irrigation allows precise water control
Irrigation is banned in all New World countries
Flood irrigation is the most water-efficient
Irrigation always increases quality
qs.e: Drip irrigation is costly to install but precise and economical, and allows water stress to be managed. Flooding wastes water; irrigation is common in the New World and permitted in many European areas; too much water gives high yields and diluted grapes.

qs.q: What aromas do Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé Sauvignons show?
o: Green apple and asparagus, often with wet pebbles
Ripe passion fruit and pineapple, with elderflower
Vanilla, coconut and toast from new barrels
Honey, dried apricot and candied orange zest
qs.e: Sauvignon Blanc from Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé in the Loire shows elegance and restraint. The cool climate gives green apple and asparagus, often with a hint of wet pebbles. Ripe passion fruit and pineapple suggest Marlborough or sunnier climates; vanilla and coconut come from oak; honey and dried apricot from noble rot or age.

qs.q: Why is Pinot Noir rarely used for high-volume inexpensive wines?
o: Hard to grow, likes cool climates; colour and tannin extract poorly at high yields
European law bans it from wines without a geographical indication and table wines
It has very thick skins and hard tannins, needing long, costly maturation
It ripens too late for the warm climates where volume wine is made
qs.e: Pinot Noir is rarely used for high-volume inexpensive wines: it is hard to grow, prefers cool climates (whereas these regions are warm) and at high yields it is hard to extract enough colour and tannin from its thin skin. It is not banned, not thick-skinned (thin) and ripens early, not late.

qs.q: Why is establishing a vineyard expensive?
o: Land, soil preparation, vines and trellis, with years before any return
Vines are bought already fruiting, with three harvests guaranteed
Because grapes are taxed from the moment the vineyard is planted
It isn't expensive if machine harvesting is chosen from the start
qs.e: Establishing a vineyard is very expensive: land is not cheap, especially in a region famed for premium wine; the soil must be prepared, vines bought and planted, and any trellis built. And it takes many years to see a return, as young vines do not crop straight away. Vines do not arrive already fruiting, grapes are not taxed as such, and it is expensive.

qs.q: Which traditional French term is more often seen on labels instead of AOP?
o: Appellation d'origine contrôlée (AC/AOC)
Vin de Pays (with the region's name)
Vin Délimité de Qualité Supérieure (VDQS)
Indication Géographique Protégée (IGP)
qs.e: The French for PDO is Appellation d'origine protégée (AOP), but the traditional term Appellation d'origine contrôlée (AC or AOC) is more widely seen on labels. One plot is often covered by both a generic and a more prestigious appellation, and each year the producer chooses which to use, often depending on vintage quality. Vin de Pays and IGP denote PGI wines; Vin de France wines without a GI.

qs.q: When can Beaujolais Nouveau be released?
o: On the third Thursday of November after the vintage
On the first Thursday of October, as soon as fermentation ends
On 1 January after the vintage
On St Martin's Day, 11 November
qs.e: Beaujolais Nouveau cannot be released to consumers until the third Thursday in November after the vintage, and cannot be sold by growers or négociants after the following 31 August. It can only be of Beaujolais or Beaujolais Villages quality: the ten crus cannot be sold this way. 1 January, Easter or right after harvest are wrong.

qs.q: Which Loire / main grape pairing is correct?
o: Savennières / Chenin Blanc
Chinon / Gamay
Pouilly-Fumé / Chardonnay
Muscadet / Sauvignon Blanc
qs.e: Savennières (Anjou) is famous for long-lived dry Chenin Blanc. Chinon is a Cabernet Franc red, Pouilly-Fumé a Central Vineyards Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadet a Melon Blanc white.

qs.q: How is Muscat used in Southern France?
o: For sweet fortified wines, sometimes dry grapey wines
Only for traditional-method sparkling wines, as at Limoux
Only for pale, aromatic rosés to drink young
To soften Carignan's tannins in red blends
qs.e: The most planted local white varieties are Muscat and Grenache Blanc. Muscat is used for sweet fortified wines but sometimes also for dry wines with aromatic, grapey aromas. To soften Carignan's tannins, some producers use semi-carbonic maceration instead.

qs.q: What is the term 'feinherb' on a German label?
o: A non-legal alternative to 'halbtrocken', for those who feel that term sounds inferior
A legal term for bone-dry wines under 4 g/L, drier than 'trocken', introduced in 2021
A legal synonym for Trockenbeerenauslese, used mainly in the Pfalz and Rheingau
It denotes a legal grand cru, recognised by German law as the top level
qs.e: German labels may state sweetness: trocken for dry and halbtrocken for off-dry or medium. Some producers feel halbtrocken has a negative association with lower-quality wines and use feinherb instead, which, unlike the other two, is not legally defined. Many wines give no sweetness indication, but it can often be deduced from the category (BA, TBA, Eiswein always sweet) or alcohol (low alcohol = probably sweet).

qs.q: In which Austrian region does Sauvignon Blanc have a growing reputation?
o: Styria
Wachau
Weinviertel
Neusiedlersee
qs.e: Other widely planted varieties in Austria are Chardonnay, Müller-Thurgau and Sauvignon Blanc, the last with a growing reputation especially in the southern region of Steiermark (Styria), one of the four wine-producing federal states. Wachau is known for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, Weinviertel for Grüner Veltliner, Neusiedlersee for botrytised sweet wines.

qs.q: Even in the wetter west of Greece, why can vines suffer water stress?
o: Because there is almost no rain in the growing season
Over-fertile soils push the canopy, which uses up all the water
Because all the rain falls as hail
Because the vines are basket-trained low
qs.e: Greece has a hot Mediterranean climate, with rain concentrated in winter. Even in the wetter areas of the west, the almost complete lack of rain during the growing season can cause water stress. It shows that how rainfall is spread through the year matters more than the annual total. Basket training is specific to Santorini and protects against wind.

qs.q: In which two styles is Barbera usually made?
o: Young and fruity unoaked, or barrel-aged with spice
Sweet and spritzy like Moscato, or dry and tannic like Barolo
A light rosé served chilled, or a sweet passito from dried grapes
Traditional-method sparkling, or still red aged in amphora
qs.e: Barbera is typically made in two styles: youthful and fruity without oak, or barrel-aged for spicy flavours. With high acidity and low tannin it takes oak well, which adds structure. Barbera and Dolcetto can be drunk young, but the best age for several years. It is not sweet, sparkling, rosé or white.

qs.q: What is Tempranillo called in Penedès?
o: Ull de Llebre
Cencibel
Mazuelo
Monastrell
qs.e: Penedès is a large DO just south-west of Barcelona, from the coast into the hills, with three climatic zones: the hottest Mediterranean coastal plain, slightly cooler but warm inland valleys, and moderate hills up to 800 m. This allows many styles and grapes. The most planted whites are the Cava grapes plus Chardonnay, Sauvignon and Gewürztraminer; the most planted blacks are Merlot, Cabernet, Tempranillo (here Ull de Llebre) and Pinot Noir. Cencibel is its La Mancha name; Mazuelo is Rioja's Cariñena.

qs.q: Which grapes make Alentejo's typical red blend?
o: Aragonez and Trincadeira, often with Alicante Bouschet
Baga and Bical, as in the Bairrada tradition
Touriga Franca and Tinto Cão, as in the Douro
Jaen and Encruzado, the typical grapes of the Dão
qs.e: Alentejo's typical red blend uses Aragonez (another name for Tempranillo) and Trincadeira, a drought-tolerant grape with spicy red berry flavours and high tannin. Alicante Bouschet, high in colour and tannin, is also used, and Touriga Nacional and Syrah have increased recently. The wines are typically deep, with high but soft tannins, full body and expressive ripe fruit. Baga and Bical are Bairrada's; Touriga Franca and Tinta Cão the Douro's; Jaen and Encruzado Dão's.

qs.q: What is Mendoza's highest area?
o: Uco Valley (900–1,500 m)
Luján de Cuyo (1,500-2,000 m)
Eastern Mendoza (800–1,200 m)
San Rafael (1,200–1,800 m)
qs.e: Uco Valley, south-west of Mendoza, is a source of high-quality fruit, with vineyards at 900-1,500 m, Mendoza's highest. Cool nights retain acidity and fresh fruit, and the wines sometimes show floral notes. Chardonnay, Torrontés, Sauvignon, Malbec, Cabernet, Merlot and Tempranillo flourish, and some sites are cool enough for Pinot Noir. It includes Tupungato, a high area increasingly recognised. Eastern Mendoza is low and volume-focused; San Rafael is low; Maipú is lower than Luján.

qs.q: Which of these terms is a category in South Africa's Wine of Origin scheme?
o: Ward
Zone
Sub-region
AVA
qs.e: South Africa's Wine of Origin scheme has four levels: Geographical Unit, Region, District and Ward (the smallest). Zones and sub-regions belong to other systems (e.g. Australia, Chile), AVA to the USA.

qs.q: Which statement about New Zealand reds is correct?
o: Pinot Noir: vibrant fruit, fine ripe tannins, often high alcohol, regional styles; Merlot the second red, blended with Cabernet; Syrah closer to the Rhône than to hot Australia
Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted red, especially in Central Otago, where it gives tannic, austere wines; Pinot Noir is marginal and used only for traditional-method sparkling
New Zealand Syrah is full, sweet and jammy like the Barossa's, with very high alcohol and American oak; Merlot is grown only in the South Island
Merlot is made only in the South Island, as the North is too hot; Pinot Noir is always light and vegetal, with green tannins and low alcohol
qs.e: Pinot Noir, the second most planted variety after Sauvignon, is grown throughout the South Island and in a few North Island sites: vibrant fruit, fine ripe tannins, soft texture and often quite high alcohol, with distinct regional styles. Merlot, though far less planted than Pinot, is the second red by volume; Cabernet is often added for tannin and cassis in Bordeaux-style blends, noted for pure fruit. These varieties are concentrated in the warmer North Island. Syrah performs best in warmer sites and makes elegant wines closer to the Rhône than to hot Australia; plantings are small but increasing.

qs.q: What do Cartizze and Rive indicate for Prosecco?
o: Wines from exceptional sites in Conegliano-Valdobbiadene DOCG
Sweet Prosecco versions with at least 30 g/L residual sugar
Proseccos made by the traditional method and aged on lees
Rosé Proseccos from Glera and Pinot Nero, aged for longer
qs.e: Prosecco has two zones: Prosecco DOC, covering much of Veneto and Friuli, and the higher-quality Conegliano-Valdobbiadene DOCG on steep limestone hills between those two towns north-west of Venice. Within the DOCG, Cartizze and Rive indicate wines from exceptional sites. The grape, once also called Prosecco, is now Glera, to protect the two appellations. These terms do not mean sweetness, traditional method or rosé: Prosecco is tank-made.

qs.q: Where do California's best sparkling wines come from?
o: Cool areas: Carneros, Anderson Valley
The Central Valley, where high yields cut the cost of base wines
Lodi, thanks to its sandy soils and old Zinfandel vines
Eastern Paso Robles, the hottest and sunniest area
qs.e: California makes the vast majority of US sparkling wine. The best come from cool areas such as Los Carneros AVA and Anderson Valley AVA, where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay keep their acidity. They use the traditional method, often with long lees ageing (five years is not uncommon), giving concentrated, complex flavours balanced by high acidity. Large volumes of cheap wine are tank-made or carbonated, often medium-sweet to sweet, from warm high-yielding areas like the Central Valley. Lodi and eastern Paso Robles are warm still-wine areas.

qs.q: Why is albariza soil vital in Jerez?
o: Very chalky: drains well yet holds water for dry summers
Rich in red clay and iron, giving Palomino colour and tannin
Dark and volcanic, it stores daytime heat and releases it at night
Sandy and fertile, allowing very high yields of very sweet grapes
qs.e: Jerez is coastal, so annual rainfall is high for Spain, but very little falls in the growing season. Albariza is what lets the vine cope: a white soil very high in chalk that drains well, yet its depth and excellent water-holding capacity store winter rain to sustain vines through hot, dry summers. After harvest, pits are dug between rows to trap water, and in summer the surface forms a hard crust that limits evaporation. It is not red clay, volcanic or fertile sand.

qs.q: What makes true Tawny Ports differ from Ruby?
o: Only the ageing: long oxidation in pipes, giving orange colour and nut and caramel notes
Different grapes, mainly white ones like Malvasia, and longer fermentation to 12%
A longer, hotter fermentation in lagares, with riper, partly dried grapes
Adding cane sugar and caramel before bottling for sweetness
qs.e: True Tawny Ports are made exactly like rubies: same grapes, same winemaking. The colour and flavour differences come entirely from maturation: long oxidative ageing in barrels called pipes. The wine turns garnet, then tawny (only the oldest go fully brown); primary fruit fades to raisin with walnut, coffee, chocolate and caramel. The deposit forms during wood ageing, so little treatment is needed before bottling, and they are fully developed on release: no gain from bottle ageing.
